questiontext.text: How does insertion sort build up a sorted result?

answer.text: It grows a sorted prefix, taking each next element and shifting larger sorted elements right to insert it into place

feedback.text: Correct — like sorting a hand of cards.

answer.text: It repeatedly selects the minimum of the unsorted part

feedback.text: That describes selection sort.

answer.text: It compares and swaps only adjacent elements pass after pass

feedback.text: That describes bubble sort.
That describes merge sort.

generalfeedback.text: Insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix on the left; each new element is inserted into its correct spot by shifting larger elements one position right.

questiontext.text: What is insertion sort's best-case time complexity on an already-sorted array?

feedback.text: Correct — each element only needs one comparison and no shifts, so it is adaptive.
That is the worst/average case; on sorted input insertion sort is O(n).
Insertion sort does not divide the problem logarithmically.
You still must scan all n elements once.

generalfeedback.text: On sorted or nearly-sorted input, each element is already at or near its place, so insertion sort runs in O(n) — it is adaptive.

feedback.text: Correct — a reverse-sorted array forces every new element to shift past all previous ones.
That is the best case on sorted input, not the worst case.
Shifting elements one at a time makes it quadratic in the worst case.
You must at least touch every element.

generalfeedback.text: In the worst case (reverse-sorted input) each of the n elements shifts past up to n prior elements, giving O(n^2).

feedback.text: Correct — it stops shifting on a strict "greater than", so equal keys keep their original order.
Insertion sort inserts after equal elements, preserving relative order, so it is stable.

questiontext.text: Insertion sort is an online algorithm: it can sort a list as elements arrive one at a time.

feedback.text: Correct — each new element is inserted into the already-sorted prefix, so it handles streaming input.
Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and can absorb each new element as it arrives, so it is online.

questiontext.text: An algorithm that runs faster when the input is already partly sorted is called ______ (one English word). Insertion sort has this property.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct — the property is "adaptive".

questiontext.text: Which statements about insertion sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is adaptive, running in O(n) on nearly-sorted input

feedback.text: Yes — fewer shifts when data is nearly ordered.

answer.text: It is stable and in-place (O(1) extra space)

feedback.text: Yes — equal keys keep order and it sorts within the array.

answer.text: Its worst-case time is O(n log n)

feedback.text: No — the worst case is O(n^2).

answer.text: It cannot process input arriving one element at a time

feedback.text: No — insertion sort is online and handles streaming input.

generalfeedback.text: Insertion sort: adaptive (O(n) best case), stable, in-place, online; worst/average case O(n^2).

questiontext.text: When is insertion sort a particularly good choice?

answer.text: For small arrays or nearly-sorted data, and as the base case inside faster divide-and-conquer sorts

feedback.text: Correct — its low overhead and adaptivity shine on small or almost-sorted inputs.

answer.text: For sorting very large random arrays where asymptotic speed matters most

feedback.text: No — O(n^2) is too slow there; use an O(n log n) sort.

answer.text: When you specifically need to minimize the number of writes

feedback.text: No — that is selection sort's niche; insertion sort can do many shifts.

generalfeedback.text: Insertion sort excels on small or nearly-sorted inputs and is often the cutoff base case in quicksort/merge sort implementations.
